e: VPC Flow Logs publish to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and Kinesis Data Firehose can stream a log group to OpenSearch Service in near real time through a subscription filter. CloudTrail doesn't receive flow logs, and Firehose (not Data Streams) is the managed delivery path to OpenSearch.

A managed node group of only Spot Instances is the cheapest way to run an infrequently used development cluster that tests resiliency, since interruptions are acceptable, and the EKS managed node group lets EKS manage all the nodes. Self-managed Auto Scaling groups aren't managed by EKS, and On-Demand costs more.

A customer managed KMS key with SSE-KMS gives the company full control to create, rotate, and disable keys with little effort. SSE-S3 and AWS managed keys don't allow that control, and manual EC2 re-encryption is operationally heavy.

Create the bucket with S3 Object Lock and a default 30-day retention period to protect the backups for 30 days, and add a lifecycle rule to expire the objects after 30 days so they're deleted automatically. Lifecycle policies can't protect objects, and tags or versioning alone don't enforce retention.

DataSync can copy continuously (scheduled) from the source S3 bucket to both the EFS file system and the other S3 bucket, and with the transfer mode set to transfer only data that has changed, files are overwritten only when the source changes, with minimal overhead. Transferring all data re-copies everything, and Lambda or EC2 scripts need more work.

A customer managed KMS key lets the company control key rotation (enable automatic rotation or set it as needed) and is used directly to encrypt EBS volumes with minimal effort. AWS managed key rotation can't be controlled, imported key material needs manual rotation, and AWS owned keys aren't visible or controllable.

An IAM policy that allows only encrypted EBS volume creation prevents new violations, and AWS Config detects noncompliant (unencrypted) volumes while Systems Manager Automation remediates them, all managed with minimal administration. Macie and Inspector don't detect unencrypted EBS volumes.

Moving the web tier to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB and the database to an RDS Multi-AZ deployment improves resiliency with minimal application changes (still MySQL). Lambda or DynamoDB would require rewriting, and a database in an Auto Scaling group isn't practical.

AWS Local Zones extend the VPC from eu-central-1 to metro locations near users and can host applications with single-digit millisecond latency in places where the Region can't be used. CloudFront edge locations don't host applications, and Wavelength Zones are for 5G mobile networks.

RDS Proxy pools and shares connections so unpredictable Lambda concurrency doesn't overload the database, and because the DB instance is private, the Lambda functions must run inside the VPC to reach the proxy. Custom endpoints don't pool connections, and Lambda outside the VPC can't reach a private database.

A transit gateway with VPC attachments and VPN attachments for the on-premises locations acts as a scalable hub, so new accounts and VPCs just attach with simple routing and low administrative overhead. Peering meshes, EC2 VPN appliances, or a central VPC with peering don't scale well.

Amazon Forecast is a managed time-series forecasting service that needs no ML experience: train a predictor on the historical data in S3, and call it from a Lambda function to produce predictions. SageMaker requires ML knowledge.

Create the users and the developer and administrator groups in IAM Identity Center, define permission sets with the right policies, and assign the groups with those permission sets to the accounts. New hires are added to the group, which is the least operational overhead. Per-account users or per-user permissions don't scale.

An AWS Config managed rule (encrypted-volumes) continuously evaluates whether EBS volumes are encrypted and flags noncompliant ones, with little cost or configuration. Custom scripts on Lambda or Fargate and tag-based reviews need more effort.

S3 multipart uploads upload parts of large files in parallel to scale upload throughput, and fetching multiple byte ranges of an object in parallel scales download throughput to the EC2 instances. Access points, multiple buckets, and random prefixes don't increase throughput for single large objects.

EFS is a shared file system with strong consistency for all mounted instances across AZs, and S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency, so with Cache-Control no-cache and CloudFront the new content is delivered as soon as it changes. Volume gateways and EBS can't be shared this way, and DataSync isn't continuous consistent sharing.

Latency-based routing (an A record, alias to the ALBs) sends each user to the Region with the lowest network latency, giving the best-performing experience. Geolocation and geoproximity route by location rather than measured latency, and CNAME records can't be used at the zone apex or for ALB aliases like A alias records.

Spreading the Auto Scaling group across three AZs makes the web tier highly available, and migrating the embedded NoSQL database to DynamoDB (using DMS) gives a managed, eventually consistent (by default) multi-AZ database with little operational work. Self-managed replication on EC2 keeps administration.

ElastiCache for Redis provides in-memory, low-latency caching for the catalog and durable, highly available storage for session and shopping cart data (Redis replication and persistence), so carts survive disconnects. Sticky sessions, OpenSearch, or a single EC2 instance don't preserve carts reliably.

CloudWatch Container Insights collects metrics and logs from the EKS cluster, and AWS X-Ray traces requests across the microservices, together providing observability to find performance issues. ElastiCache, CloudTrail, or Trusted Advisor don't trace requests.

A separate KMS key per customer with SSE-KMS encryption, and a key policy that denies decryption to everyone except a role in the customer's account, ensures each customer can decrypt only their own data and employees can't. Bucket policies can't control decryption rights, and ACM certificates aren't for data encryption.

An internet-facing ALB in a public subnet that forwards to the instance in the private subnet lets external traffic reach the web server while the instance stays private, and DNS should resolve to the ALB. NAT gateways allow only outbound connections, and private instances have no public IP.

Amazon EFS provides shared, highly available, fault-tolerant storage that works with EKS on Fargate (Fargate supports EFS but not EBS), and one file system can be mounted by many containers, with minimal overhead. EBS volumes can't be shared across Fargate pods, and cross-file-system sync is extra work.

ECS on Fargate removes server management, and an EFS volume mounted in the tasks provides fully managed persistent shared storage with no storage infrastructure to manage. EKS self-managed nodes and ECS on EC2 keep servers, and S3 can't be mounted as a volume.

Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP and routes global users to the closest healthy Region with fast failover, and it can use Network Load Balancers (which support TCP and UDP) in each Region as endpoints. ALBs don't support UDP, and CloudFront and Route 53 geolocation don't provide UDP acceleration with the same availability.
